title: Oxygen Sensing Adaptation, Range 1 (Idle/Low Load) at Limit, Bank 1
description: Porsche-specific long-term fuel-trim (mixture) adaptation code. The DME's oxygen-sensing adaptation for bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) has reached its limit - almost always because the engine is running lean and the DME can no longer add enough fuel to compensate. On the M96/M97 flat-six this is the classic 'unmetered air' code and points to an intake/vacuum leak far more often than to a bad O2 sensor. It is very frequently logged together with P1130 (bank 2).
symptoms: Hesitation or stumble, especially when cold
causes: Cracked or collapsed air-oil separator (AOS) diaphragm - the single most common cause on the flat-six
Torn intake boots, split vacuum lines, or leaking check valves
Loose/failed oil filler cap or leaking dipstick-tube seal
Dirty or failing MAF under-reporting airflow
Weak fuel delivery (failing pump, clogged filter) if lean under load
diagnosis: Read live short- and long-term fuel trims - a large positive LTFT confirms a lean condition
Smoke-test the intake tract for vacuum leaks (AOS, boots, manifold O-rings)
Inspect/replace the AOS and check crankcase vacuum with a manometer
Clean or bench-test the MAF; compare g/s against expected
Check oil-cap and dipstick-tube seals
Verify fuel pressure/volume before condemning sensors
Clear codes and road-test to confirm trims return to normal

title: Oxygen Sensing Adaptation, Range 1 (Idle/Low Load) at Limit, Bank 2
description: Bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) counterpart to P1128. The Porsche-specific long-term fuel-trim adaptation for bank 2 has reached its limit, normally because the engine is lean and cannot be enriched further. On the M96/M97 flat-six the two banks share the same intake, so P1130 nearly always appears alongside P1128 and points to a common unmetered-air source rather than a single-bank fault.
causes: Loose oil filler cap or dipstick-tube leak
diagnosis: Read fuel trims - positive LTFT on both banks points to a shared vacuum leak
Smoke-test the intake and replace the AOS if the diaphragm is torn
Clean/test the MAF
Check oil cap and tube seals
Verify fuel pressure
Clear and road-test

title: Oxygen Sensing Adaptation, Upper Load Range, Bank 1 - Above Limit
description: Porsche-specific multiplicative fuel-trim adaptation code. At higher engine load the mixture correction for bank 1 has reached its adaptation limit. Unlike the idle-range codes (P1128/P1130), this fault is weighted toward part- and full-load metering, so it points more strongly at the MAF, a large vacuum leak, or a fuel-delivery shortfall than at a small idle vacuum leak.
symptoms: Hesitation or flat spot under acceleration
causes: Dirty or failing MAF (skewed multiplicative correction)
Weak fuel delivery (pump, filter, injectors) if lean
Over-fuelling source such as a leaking injector if rich
diagnosis: Log fuel trims across the load range, not just at idle
Clean or replace the MAF and re-check the multiplicative trim
Smoke-test the intake
Verify fuel pressure/volume under load
Clear and road-test through the affected load range

title: Oxygen Sensing Adaptation, Lower Load Range, Bank 1 - Below Limit
description: Porsche-specific additive fuel-trim adaptation code for bank 1 at lower load. The additive (idle/low-load) mixture correction has hit its limit. On the M96/M97 this is part of the same lean-diagnosis family as P1128 and usually indicates unmetered air entering the intake at idle and light load.
causes: Loose oil cap or dipstick-tube seal
diagnosis: Read additive fuel-trim adaptation at idle
Smoke-test the intake and replace AOS if torn
Clean/test the MAF
Check oil cap and tube seals
Clear and road-test

title: Camshaft Adjustment (VarioCam), Bank 1 - Signal Implausible
description: Porsche-specific VarioCam code (Porsche fault 174). The measured intake camshaft position on bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) deviates from what the DME commanded, or the adjustment cannot be completed. On the M96/M97 flat-six this is the classic VarioCam wear code: worn actuator chain-guide pads, stretched cam/intermediate chains, a sticking oil-control solenoid, or low/dirty oil. Replacing VarioCam wear pads, chains, actuators and solenoids is considered normal maintenance around 60-80k miles on these engines.
causes: Worn VarioCam actuator wear pads / chain guides
Sticking or clogged camshaft oil-control solenoid (dirt in hydraulic valve)
Low oil level or degraded/wrong-grade oil
diagnosis: Read live camshaft deviation on bank 1 with a Porsche-capable tool (flag deviation beyond spec, roughly +/-6 degrees)
Check oil level and condition; confirm correct A40 / 0W-40 grade
Remove, inspect and clean the oil-control solenoid and its screen
If deviation persists, inspect VarioCam actuator, chains and wear pads (borescope or engine-out)
Replace wear pads/actuator/chains as a set if worn

title: Camshaft Adjustment (VarioCam), Bank 2 - Signal Implausible
description: Bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) counterpart to P1341 (Porsche fault 178). The VarioCam intake-cam adjustment on bank 2 is out of range or implausible. Same failure profile as bank 1: worn actuator wear pads and chains, sticking oil-control solenoid, or an oil-supply problem on the M96/M97 flat-six.
diagnosis: Read live bank 2 cam deviation
Check oil level/condition and grade
Clean or replace the bank 2 oil-control solenoid
Inspect VarioCam actuator/chains if deviation persists
Replace worn components as a set

title: Position of Camshaft in Relation to Crankshaft, Bank 1
description: Porsche-specific cam-to-crank correlation code for bank 1. The measured relationship between the bank 1 camshaft and the crankshaft is out of position - i.e. the cam timing has deviated. On the M96/M97 this usually accompanies VarioCam wear and chain stretch; a large deviation can indicate a serious timing error and warrants prompt investigation before driving hard.
causes: Cam timing deviation from worn VarioCam actuator/wear pads
diagnosis: Compare commanded vs actual cam angle and cam-to-crank correlation in live data
Check oil level/condition and cam-control solenoid operation
Inspect timing chain for stretch and tensioner/guides for wear
Verify cam/crank sensors and reluctor wheels
Mechanically verify cam timing if deviation is large

title: Position of Camshaft in Relation to Crankshaft, Bank 2
description: Bank 2 counterpart to P1340. The cam-to-crank relationship on bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) is out of position, indicating cam-timing deviation. On the M96/M97 this typically stems from VarioCam wear and cam-chain stretch on bank 2.
causes: Cam timing deviation from worn VarioCam components (bank 2)
diagnosis: Compare commanded vs actual bank 2 cam angle
Check oil and solenoid operation
Inspect chain/tensioner for wear
Verify sensors/reluctors
Mechanically verify timing if deviation is large

title: Camshaft Adjustment, Bank 1 - Output Stage (Solenoid Circuit)
description: Porsche-specific electrical fault in the bank 1 VarioCam camshaft-adjustment solenoid output-stage/circuit. Unlike P1341 (a performance/implausible-signal fault), this points to the wiring or the solenoid coil itself rather than mechanical cam-chain wear.
causes: Open, shorted or corroded solenoid wiring/connector
Loss of B+ supply or ground to the solenoid
diagnosis: Measure solenoid coil resistance against spec
Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion or damage
Check B+ supply and ground at the solenoid
Command the actuator with a scan tool and watch response
Replace the solenoid if out of spec

title: Secondary Air Injection System, Bank 2 - Insufficient Flow
description: Porsche-specific secondary-air code for bank 2 (cylinders 4-6). Where generic OBD-II uses P0413/P0411 for bank 2, the Porsche DME logs P1411, and it very commonly appears paired with the generic P0410 (bank 1). The secondary-air system pumps fresh air into the exhaust ports for ~90 seconds after a cold start to light off the catalysts; this code sets when measured air flow is implausible. Only monitored during the cold-start SAI cycle.
symptoms: Check-engine light (often after a cold start)
Brief rough idle / raised idle when cold
Buzzing air-pump noise on cold start
causes: Brittle, cracked secondary-air plastic hoses (over 80% of these codes)
Vacuum leak or failed check valve in the SAI control circuit
Carbon-clogged air passages into the heads
diagnosis: Confirm the code sets only during the cold-start SAI window
Inspect the SAI hoses for cracks/brittleness and the change-over valve for sticking
Verify the SAI pump runs on cold start (listen/measure current)
Check control vacuum and the check valve
Clear codes and re-test on a cold start

title: Secondary Air Injection System (Bank 1) - Insufficient Flow
description: Bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) secondary-air fault, usually logged alongside the Porsche-specific P1411 (bank 2). The DME sees implausible flow from the secondary-air system during the cold-start catalyst warm-up cycle. On the flat-six the classic cause is brittle cracked SAI hoses; the code is only set during the cold-start SAI window and typically causes no warm-running drivability issues.
causes: Vacuum-control leak or bad check valve
diagnosis: Verify the code sets during the cold-start SAI cycle
Inspect SAI hoses and the change-over valve
Confirm the SAI pump runs when cold
Check control vacuum and check valve
Clear and re-test cold

title: Fuel Rail/System Pressure Too Low
description: On the 987.2 direct-injection 9A1 engine, low rail pressure most often means a failing high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) or its rail-pressure sensor - the subject of a Porsche recall/service action on 2009-2011 Boxster/Cayman (and 997.2). Porsche issued a bulletin urging techs to verify the sensor before condemning the pump. Can also be a weak in-tank low-pressure supply, a metering/volume-control valve fault, or a clogged filter.
symptoms: Long crank / hard start, often worse when warm
causes: Worn or failing high-pressure fuel pump (9A1 recall item)
Faulty fuel-rail pressure sensor (check first per Porsche bulletin)
Weak in-tank low-pressure pump or clogged filter
diagnosis: Read commanded vs actual rail pressure in live data
Check the low-pressure (feed) pressure first
Follow the Porsche service bulletin: test/replace the rail-pressure SENSOR before condemning the HPFP
Inspect and test the high-pressure pump
Confirm against the recall/service action for the VIN

title: Fuel Rail/System Pressure Too High
description: On the 987.2 9A1 DFI engine, rail pressure is above the expected level. Usually a stuck or malfunctioning volume-control/pressure-regulator valve on the high-pressure pump, or a faulty rail-pressure sensor reporting incorrectly. Excess pressure can force rich running and stress injectors.
causes: Stuck volume-control / pressure-regulator valve on the HPFP
Wiring fault to the regulator valve
diagnosis: Compare commanded vs actual rail pressure
Test the volume-control / regulator valve
Inspect the rail-pressure sensor and wiring
Inspect the high-pressure pump

title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
description: The 987.2 9A1 DFI rail-pressure sensor is reading implausibly. This is the sensor Porsche specifically told technicians to check before replacing high-pressure fuel pumps during the Gen2 HPFP problems - a failing sensor mimics a failing pump. A drifting or faulty sensor corrupts the DME's fuel-pressure control loop.
causes: Faulty or drifting fuel-rail pressure sensor
Loss of reference voltage or ground
diagnosis: Compare rail-pressure sensor reading vs commanded and vs a known-good baseline
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring
Check reference voltage and ground
Test/replace the sensor before condemning the HPFP
Re-check rail-pressure control after replacement

title: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
description: The DME detected misfires across multiple or random cylinders. On the flat-six, coil packs and spark plugs are the most common cause; a shared cause (vacuum leak, low fuel pressure, secondary-air/intake fault) often produces random rather than single-cylinder misfires. A flashing CEL means active catalyst-damaging misfire - stop driving.
causes: Worn spark plugs or failing ignition coils (multiple)
Low or high fuel pressure (DFI HPFP on 987.2)
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame and per-cylinder misfire counters
Inspect plugs and coils; replace as a set if aged
Smoke-test intake for vacuum leaks
Check fuel pressure (rail pressure on DFI)
Verify MAF and fuel trims

title: Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected
description: The DME detected a misfire on cylinder 1 (bank 1, cylinders 1-3). On the flat-six, coil packs and spark plugs are the most common cause. On 987.2 DFI engines, injector and carbon issues also contribute.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: Cylinder 2 Misfire Detected
description: Misfire on cylinder 2 (bank 1, cylinders 1-3). Coil and plug are the first suspects on the flat-six; swap-testing to an adjacent cylinder quickly isolates the fault.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: Cylinder 3 Misfire Detected
description: Misfire on cylinder 3 (bank 1, cylinders 1-3). Ignition coil and spark plug are the most common causes on the flat-six.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: Cylinder 4 Misfire Detected
description: Misfire on cylinder 4 (bank 2, cylinders 4-6). Coil and plug are the first suspects on the flat-six.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: Cylinder 5 Misfire Detected
description: Misfire on cylinder 5 (bank 2, cylinders 4-6). Ignition coil and spark plug are the most common causes on the flat-six.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: Cylinder 6 Misfire Detected
description: Misfire on cylinder 6 (bank 2, cylinders 4-6). Coil and plug are the first suspects on the flat-six; swap-testing isolates the fault quickly.
diagnosis: Read freeze-frame data
Swap the coil/plug to an adjacent cylinder and see if the misfire follows
Inspect the injector
Compression/leak-down test if it persists

title: System Too Lean (Bank 1)
description: Fuel trims on bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) have gone lean beyond the correction limit. On the 987 flat-six the usual cause is unmetered air - a failed air-oil separator or an intake/vacuum leak - or a dirty MAF. Note: 987.1 M96/M97 cars often log the Porsche codes P1128/P1130 for the same lean condition, whereas 987.2 DFI cars typically set P0171/P0174.
diagnosis: Read short/long-term fuel trims (high positive LTFT confirms lean)
Smoke-test the intake and replace the AOS if torn
Clean/test the MAF
Check oil cap and tube seals
Verify fuel pressure

title: System Too Lean (Bank 2)
description: Bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) counterpart to P0171. Fuel trims are lean beyond the correction limit. Because both banks share the intake, P0174 usually appears with P0171 and points to a common unmetered-air source (AOS, vacuum leak, MAF) rather than a single-bank fault. Most characteristic of 987.2 DFI cars; 987.1 tends to log P1128/P1130.
diagnosis: Read fuel trims on both banks
Smoke-test the intake; replace AOS if torn
Clean/test the MAF
Check oil-cap and tube seals
Verify fuel pressure

title: "A" Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 1)
description: Bank 1 intake camshaft timing is more advanced than the DME commanded - a VarioCam Plus performance fault. On the 987.2 DFI 9A1 engine this generic code is the primary VarioCam timing code (the 987.1 M96/M97 tends to log the Porsche-specific P1340/P1341 instead). Usually oil-flow or actuator related.
causes: Low oil pressure or degraded/wrong-grade oil
diagnosis: Verify oil level, condition and pressure
Clean or replace the oil-control valve
Compare actual vs commanded cam angle in live data
Inspect the cam position sensor
Inspect timing components if it persists

title: "A" Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 2)
description: Bank 2 counterpart to P0011: intake cam timing over-advanced / VarioCam Plus performance fault on cylinders 4-6. On 987.2 DFI cars this generic code is the primary VarioCam timing code for bank 2; 987.1 cars typically log P1324/P1325.
causes: Low oil pressure or degraded oil
diagnosis: Verify oil level/pressure
Clean or replace the oil-control valve
Compare actual vs commanded cam angle
Inspect cam sensor
Inspect timing components if persistent

title: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A)
description: The crankshaft and bank 1 camshaft position signals are out of correlation - a possible cam-timing fault. On the flat-six this points to VarioCam/chain wear, a sticking adjuster, or a cam/crank sensor issue. Persistent correlation faults warrant mechanical timing verification.
causes: Cam timing off (chain stretch / worn tensioner)
Faulty cam or crank position sensor
diagnosis: Compare cam vs crank correlation in live data
Inspect cam/crank sensors and reluctor wheels
Check oil condition and adjuster operation
Verify cam timing mechanically if needed

title: Camshaft Position Sensor "A" Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
description: The bank 1 camshaft position sensor signal is implausible or out of range. The DME uses this signal for VarioCam control and cylinder identification; a poor signal can cause hard starts and cam-timing faults on the flat-six.
diagnosis: Inspect the sensor connector and wiring
Check the sensor air gap and reluctor condition
Compare cam signal in live data
Replace the sensor if out of spec

title: O2 Sensor Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
description: Fault in the upstream (pre-catalyst) bank 1 oxygen-sensor signal circuit. The flat-six runs wideband/heated O2 sensors that suffer heater and signal ageing; a bad upstream sensor skews fuel trims. Note a lean-adaptation code (P1128/P0171) is usually an intake leak, not the sensor - confirm the sensor is truly at fault.
causes: Aged or contaminated upstream O2 sensor
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor
Actual lean/rich condition skewing the signal
diagnosis: Read the upstream O2 signal live for switching activity
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring
Check for exhaust leaks near the sensor
Rule out a real mixture fault (trims) before replacing
Replace the sensor if lazy/dead

title: O2 Sensor Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
description: Fault in the downstream (post-catalyst) bank 1 oxygen-sensor circuit. The downstream sensor monitors catalyst efficiency; its signal should be relatively steady. A fault here is usually the sensor or wiring rather than a mixture problem.
diagnosis: Read downstream O2 live data
Inspect connector and wiring
Check for exhaust leaks
Replace the sensor if faulty

title: MAF Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
description: The mass-airflow signal is out of the expected range relative to other engine data. All 987 engines (M96/M97 and 9A1 DFI) are MAF-based, so a dirty or drifting MAF skews fuel trims and is a common trigger for lean codes (P1128/P1130 on 987.1, P0171/P0174 on 987.2).
diagnosis: Inspect and clean the MAF element (MAF-safe cleaner)
Check for intake leaks between MAF and throttle
Compare MAF g/s to expected at idle and load
Replace the MAF if it stays out of range

title: MAF Sensor Circuit Low Input
description: The MAF signal voltage/frequency is too low. On the 987 this is a dirty/failed MAF, an air-intake restriction, or a wiring problem. Low MAF causes under-fuelling and lean codes.
causes: Open or short in MAF wiring
diagnosis: Check MAF wiring and connector
Inspect and clean the sensor element
Verify the MAF reading at idle
Replace the MAF if unresponsive

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
description: The coolant-temperature signal is implausible relative to other data (e.g. doesn't track warm-up correctly). On the flat-six this is often a failing ECT sensor but can also flag a thermostat problem. A bad ECT signal skews cold-start enrichment and fan control.
diagnosis: Compare ECT vs intake-air temp at cold start (should match)
Watch ECT track smoothly during warm-up
Check wiring/connector
Verify coolant level and thermostat operation

title: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temp Below Regulating Temperature)
description: The engine did not reach the expected operating temperature within the expected time - classic symptom of a stuck-open thermostat on the flat-six. The DME calculates that coolant should have reached the thermostat's regulating temperature and it has not. Common as thermostats age on the 987.
diagnosis: Watch coolant temp reach and hold the regulating temperature (~87 C) in live data
Feel for uneven warm-up / early lower-hose heating
Verify the ECT sensor reads accurately
Replace the thermostat if it opens early / won't close

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)
description: The DME compared upstream and downstream O2 signals on bank 1 and calculated that the catalytic converter is no longer converting efficiently. On the 987 this can be a genuinely worn catalyst (age/mileage or a prior misfire/oil-fouling event) or a lazy downstream O2 sensor. Rule out upstream faults (misfire, lean codes) that damage cats first.
causes: Prior misfire or oil consumption contaminating the cat
diagnosis: Compare upstream vs downstream O2 switching (downstream should be steady)
Confirm no active misfire or lean/rich codes first
Check for exhaust leaks
Test/replace the downstream O2 sensor before condemning the cat

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
description: Bank 2 counterpart to P0420: the bank 2 catalytic converter is calculated to be converting inefficiently. Same diagnostic approach - confirm the downstream O2 sensor and rule out upstream faults before replacing the converter.
diagnosis: Compare bank 2 upstream vs downstream O2 signals
Rule out misfire and mixture codes first
Check for exhaust leaks
Test the downstream sensor before replacing the cat

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Small Leak)
description: The evaporative-emissions system detected a small leak. On the 987 the overwhelmingly common cause is a loose or worn fuel-filler cap; other causes are cracked EVAP hoses or a leaking purge/vent valve. No drivability effect but it will keep the CEL on.
causes: Loose, worn or wrong fuel-filler cap (most common)
diagnosis: Inspect and reseat/replace the fuel cap first
Smoke-test the EVAP system to locate the leak
Check purge and vent valve operation
Clear the code and confirm it stays off

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Large Leak)
description: The EVAP system detected a large/gross leak. On the 987 this is most often a fuel cap left loose or not sealing, or a disconnected/split EVAP hose. Larger than the P0442 threshold but still no real drivability impact.
causes: Fuel cap loose, missing, or not sealing
diagnosis: Check the fuel cap and filler-neck seal first
Smoke-test to find the large leak
Inspect EVAP hoses and valves
Clear and confirm the fix

title: Idle Air Control System RPM Higher Than Expected
description: Idle speed is higher than the DME's target. On the drive-by-wire 987 there is no separate idle-air valve, so a high idle almost always means unmetered air reaching the engine - a vacuum leak or a dirty throttle body - the same family of causes behind the lean adaptation codes.
symptoms: Idle doesn't settle after start or on lift-off
causes: Dirty throttle body / stuck throttle plate
diagnosis: Smoke-test the intake for vacuum leaks
Clean the throttle body and check the plate seals
Inspect the AOS
Verify throttle-position live data and adaptation

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor "D"/"E" Voltage Correlation
description: The two accelerator-pedal position sensors disagree with each other. On the drive-by-wire 987 the DME uses redundant pedal sensors; when they lose correlation the DME defaults to reduced power / limp mode as a safety measure. Usually the pedal sensor assembly or its wiring.
causes: Loss of reference voltage or ground
diagnosis: Read both pedal-sensor voltages live - they should track proportionally
Inspect the pedal connector and wiring for corrosion
Check reference voltages and grounds
Replace the pedal sensor assembly if signals don't correlate

title: "A" Camshaft Position Slow Response (Bank 1)
description: Variable valve timing (VarioCam) fault: during a commanded camshaft phase change, the actual position of the "A" camshaft on bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) responds too slowly to match the position the DME requested. Usually oil-flow or actuator related rather than a failed sensor.
causes: Low oil level, degraded oil, or wrong viscosity
Clogged camshaft oil control valve (VarioCam solenoid) or its filter screen
Stretched timing chain or worn chain tensioner/guides
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid
diagnosis: Check oil level and condition; confirm correct grade (Porsche A40 / 0W-40)
Scan live data: compare commanded vs actual cam timing during a phase change
Test the camshaft oil control valve solenoid (resistance + actuation) and clean its screen
Inspect timing chain for stretch and the tensioner/guides for wear
Check solenoid wiring/connector continuity and the cam sensor signal
Clear the code and road-test to confirm the fix

title: "B" Camshaft Position Slow Response (Bank 1)
description: Variable valve timing (VarioCam) fault: during a commanded camshaft phase change, the actual position of the "B" camshaft on bank 1 (cylinders 1-3) responds too slowly to match the position the DME requested. Usually oil-flow or actuator related rather than a failed sensor.
causes: Low oil level, degraded oil, or wrong viscosity
Clogged camshaft oil control valve (VarioCam solenoid) or its filter screen
Stretched timing chain or worn chain tensioner/guides
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid
diagnosis: Check oil level and condition; confirm correct grade (Porsche A40 / 0W-40)
Scan live data: compare commanded vs actual cam timing during a phase change
Test the camshaft oil control valve solenoid (resistance + actuation) and clean its screen
Inspect timing chain for stretch and the tensioner/guides for wear
Check solenoid wiring/connector continuity and the cam sensor signal
Clear the code and road-test to confirm the fix

title: "A" Camshaft Position Slow Response (Bank 2)
description: Variable valve timing (VarioCam) fault: during a commanded camshaft phase change, the actual position of the "A" camshaft on bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) responds too slowly to match the position the DME requested. Usually oil-flow or actuator related rather than a failed sensor.
causes: Low oil level, degraded oil, or wrong viscosity
Clogged camshaft oil control valve (VarioCam solenoid) or its filter screen

Scan live data: compare commanded vs actual cam timing during a phase change
Test the camshaft oil control valve solenoid (resistance + actuation) and clean its screen
Inspect timing chain for stretch and the tensioner/guides for wear
Check solenoid wiring/connector continuity and the cam sensor signal
Clear the code and road-test to confirm the fix

title: "B" Camshaft Position Slow Response (Bank 2)
description: Variable valve timing (VarioCam) fault: during a commanded camshaft phase change, the actual position of the "B" camshaft on bank 2 (cylinders 4-6) responds too slowly to match the position the DME requested. Usually oil-flow or actuator related rather than a failed sensor.

Inspect timing chain for stretch and the tensioner/guides for wear

Clear the code and road-test to confirm the fix

title: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 1)
description: The DME detected an electrical fault in the Bank 1 intake camshaft adjuster (VarioCam oil-control solenoid) circuit.
causes: Failed camshaft oil-control valve / VarioCam solenoid
Clogged oil galleries to the adjuster
diagnosis: Read live cam-adjustment data with a Porsche-capable tool
Check oil level and condition
Measure solenoid resistance and circuit continuity
Inspect connector for corrosion
Command/test actuator operation

title: "A" Camshaft Position Timing Over-Retarded (Bank 1)
description: Bank 1 camshaft timing is more retarded than commanded — a VarioCam performance fault.
diagnosis: Verify oil level and pressure
Clean or replace the oil control valve
Compare actual vs commanded cam angle
Inspect timing mechanically if it persists

title: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 1)
description: Electrical fault in the Bank 1 exhaust camshaft adjuster (oil-control solenoid) circuit.
causes: Loss of reference voltage or ground
diagnosis: Inspect the camshaft adjuster solenoid connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Measure sensor resistance/voltage against specification
Check reference voltage and ground at the connector
Compare live data to a known-good value
Replace the sensor if out of spec

title: "B" Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced (Bank 1)
description: Bank 1 exhaust camshaft timing over-advanced — a VarioCam performance fault.
diagnosis: Verify oil level and pressure
Replace oil control valve
Compare actual vs commanded cam angle

title: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor B)
description: Crank/cam correlation fault on Bank 1, exhaust-cam sensor.
diagnosis: Compare cam vs crank correlation
Inspect sensors and reluctors
Verify cam timing if needed

title: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 2 Sensor A)
description: Crank/cam correlation fault on Bank 2, intake-cam sensor.
diagnosis: Compare cam vs crank correlation
Inspect sensors and reluctors
